summary: Defines a mobility option for Proxy Mobile IPv6 that carries information about the access network a mobile node is attached to. With it, the local mobility anchor can apply access-network- and operator-specific handling or policing to the node's traffic. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: When a device roams onto a different operator's network, the operator may want to treat its traffic differently. This RFC lets the access gateway tell the mobility anchor which network the device is on and who runs it, so that a policy can be applied without the anchor having to ask anyone else.

subtitle: Telling the mobility anchor which access network a mobile device is on, so the operator can treat it differently.

tldr.problem: In Proxy Mobile IPv6 the mobile access gateway already tells the local mobility anchor what kind of radio technology the device is on, but that is not enough to apply a policy: an operator needs to know which access network and which operator it is attached to.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a mobility option, type 52, carrying up to three sub-options: the name of the access network and the access point, the geographic coordinates of the network, and the identity of the operator running it.
tldr.outcome: The two ends negotiate the information with three configuration flags, the anchor echoes back the sub-options it accepted, and the option is kept inside the Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain unless the subscriber agrees otherwise.

today: RFC 6757 is a Proposed Standard and the option it defines was later extended by RFC 7563, which adds extensions to the Proxy Mobile IPv6 Access Network Identifier option. The mobility option type 52 and the three sub-option types it registers remain the way access network information travels from the access gateway to the mobility anchor.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 can be used for supporting network-based mobility management in various types of network deployment. Network architectures such as service provider Wi-Fi access aggregation, or a Wireless Local Area Network integrated with a mobile packet core, are examples where Proxy Mobile IPv6 is a component of the overall architecture.

Some of these architectures require the local mobility anchor to provide differentiated services and policing of traffic to the mobile nodes based on the access network to which they are attached. Policy systems in mobility architectures, such as the Policy and Charging Control Framework and the Access Network Discovery and Selection Function in 3GPP systems, allow the configuration of policy rules with conditions based on access network information. For example, the service treatment for the mobile node's traffic may be different when it is attached to an access network owned by the home operator than when it is owned by a roaming partner, and it can be different based on the configured service set identifiers in the case of access networks based on IEEE 802.11. Other examples of location services include the operator's ability to display a location-specific web page or apply a tariff based on the location.

The Proxy Mobile IPv6 specification requires the Access Technology Type option to be carried from the mobile access gateway to the local mobility anchor. That option is mandatory. However, the access technology type alone is not necessarily sufficient for a suitable policy to be applied at the local mobility anchor, so additional access-network-related information is needed there. Learning the identity of the access network operator may not be possible for a local mobility anchor without the support of an additional policy framework able to provide the information out of band, and such a framework may not be required for all Proxy Mobile IPv6 deployments, so an alternative approach for optionally carrying the information is required.

This document defines a new mobility option, the Access Network Identifier option, and its sub-options, which can be used by the mobile access gateway to signal access network information to the local mobility anchor. The specific details of how the local mobility anchor uses the information are out of scope. The information is intended for use between infrastructure nodes providing mobile management service and is not exposed to outside entities, which ensures that the location of the network to which the mobile node is attached, or any other access-network-specific information, is not revealed to other mobile nodes within the Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain or to nodes outside it. However, the location and access information may be exposed to specific parties outside the domain based on an agreement approved by the subscriber; otherwise it must not be exposed in the absence of such agreements. If the location information is to be exposed outside the domain, that must be done using a Presence Information Data Format Location Object carrying the usage rules to which the subscriber has agreed. The mobility option is optional and not mandatory for the Proxy Mobile IPv6 protocol, while the Access Technology Type option continues to be mandatory and always needs to be carried.
sections.plainLanguage: Knowing that a device is on a Wi-Fi network is not the same as knowing which Wi-Fi network. The anchor needs the second to apply the operator's rules, and the RFC defines a way to carry it.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
All the mobility-related terms used in this document are to be interpreted as defined in the Proxy Mobile IPv6 specifications. The document also uses two abbreviations of its own.

The Service Set Identifier identifies the name of the IEEE 802.11 network and differentiates one network from another. The Operator-Identifier is the Structure of Management Information Network Management Private Enterprise Code of the IANA-maintained Private Enterprise Numbers registry. It identifies the operator running the network attached to a specific interface of the mobile access gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: Two names are defined. The service set identifier is the name of the wireless network. The operator identifier is a number from a public registry that stands for the company running the network.

sections.title: The Access Network Identifier Option
sections.content:
The Access Network Identifier option is a mobility header option used to exchange information related to the access network between a local mobility anchor and a mobile access gateway. The option can be included in both Proxy Binding Update and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement messages, and there must not be more than a single instance of this mobility option in a mobility message. The option must contain one or more Access Network Identifier sub-options.

The option has a Type field, which must be set to the value 52, and a Length field, an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the length in octets of the option excluding the Type and Length fields. The alignment requirement for this option is 4n.

The sub-option format has an ANI Type field, an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the type of the sub-option, and an ANI Length field, an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the number of octets needed to encode the option data, excluding the ANI Type and ANI Length fields. The types defined by this specification are 0 for reserved, 1 for the Network-Identifier sub-option, 2 for the Geo-Location sub-option, and 3 for the Operator-Identifier sub-option.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a small header followed by one or more sub-options, each with a type number and a length. A message may carry only one copy of the option, but the option may carry several different sub-options.

sections.title: The Three Sub-Options
sections.content:
The Network-Identifier sub-option carries the name of the access network to which the mobile node is attached, such as an SSID in the case of an IEEE 802.11 access network or a PLMN identifier in the case of 3GPP access. There must be no more than a single instance of this sub-option in any Access Network Identifier option. Its ANI Type is 1, and its ANI Length, the total length excluding the ANI Type and ANI Length fields, can be in the range of 5 to 32 octets.

The sub-option also carries a 1-bit flag saying whether the network name is encoded in UTF-8, a reserved field that must be set to zero on sending and ignored on receipt, an 8-bit network name length that must not be set to zero, the network name itself, an 8-bit access point name length which must be zero if the access point name is not included, and the access point name. The type of the network name depends on the access technology: for 802.11 access it must be the SSID, for 3GPP access it is the PLMN identifier, and for 3GPP2 access it is the Access Network Identifier. When encoding the PLMN identifier, both the Mobile Network Code and the Mobile Country Code must be 3 digits, so a 2-digit network code must be preceded with a zero, and the encoding must be UTF-8. The access point name is the name of the physical access point to which the mobile node is attached. While the network name identifies the operator's access network, the access point name identifies a specific device in it, and in some deployments it can be set to the MAC address of the device or another unique identifier that the operator's policy systems can use to identify it unambiguously. It is carried in UTF-8.

The Geo-Location sub-option carries the geographic location of the network to which the mobile node is attached, as known to the mobile access gateway. Its ANI Type is 2 and its ANI Length must be 6. It encodes the coordinates of an ellipsoid point based on the coordinate reference system specified in the World Geodetic System 1984. The latitude is a 24-bit value encoded as a two's complement fixed point number with 9 whole bits, where positive degrees correspond to the Northern Hemisphere and negative degrees to the Southern Hemisphere, and the value ranges from -90 to +90 degrees. The longitude is a 24-bit value encoded in the same way, ranging from -180 to +180 degrees.

The Operator-Identifier sub-option carries the operator identifier of the access network. Its ANI Type is 3. An 8-bit Op-ID Type field gives the type of the identifier, with 0 reserved, 1 meaning a variable-length Private Enterprise Number encoded in network byte order, and 2 meaning the realm of the operator. The maximum PEN value depends on the ANI Length and is calculated as 2 to the power of (ANI_length minus 1) times 8, minus 1, so an ANI Length of 4 allows PENs from 0 to 2^24-1, that is from 0 to 16777215, using 3 octets of operator identifier space. A realm of the operator is required to be unique, is piggybacked on the administration of the DNS namespace, meets the syntactic requirements of the Preferred Name Syntax, and is encoded as US-ASCII; 3GPP specifications also define realm names that can be used to convey PLMN identifiers. The operator identifier is up to 253 octets, and must not be empty for the identifiers defined in this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Three pieces of information, each optional. Which network and which access point the device is on. Where that network physically is, as a latitude and longitude. And a number or a DNS name for the company that runs it.

sections.title: Protocol Considerations
sections.content:
The conceptual Binding Update List entry data structure maintained by the mobile access gateway must be extended to store the access-network-related information elements associated with the current session, with parameters defined for the Network-Identifier, the Operator-Identifier and the Geo-Location. If the mobile access gateway is configured to support the option, it should include it with the specific sub-options in all Proxy Binding Update messages, including those for lifetime extension and for deregistration, that it sends to the local mobility anchor, and it should include the sub-options it is configured to carry.

The access network information elements are typically configured statically on the mobile access gateway on a per-interface basis, for example access point AP-1 attached through interface-1 with a given SSID and geo-location. In some deployments the information can also be obtained dynamically, such as through the DHCP Relay Agent Information option: when the mobile node sends a DHCP request, the access points typically add the SSID information to Option 82, and the mobile access gateway can parse it to obtain the SSID name. It can also be obtained from the DHCPv6 GeoLoc option. The details of how the gateway obtains the elements are access technology and deployment specific and outside the scope of the document.

Each sub-option has its own configuration flag. If the flag for a sub-option is set to 1, the gateway should include that sub-option in the Proxy Binding Update; if the gateway is unable to obtain the information it must not include the sub-option. The access network operator should obtain an identifier from the Private Enterprise Number registry in order for the gateway to carry the operator identifier, and if the operator has not obtained one, or the gateway cannot learn the identity for other administrative reasons, the gateway must not include the sub-option.

If the gateway had included the option in the Proxy Binding Update, the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement received from the local mobility anchor should contain the option with the specific sub-options. If the gateway receives an acknowledgement with a successful status value but without the option, it should log the event and, based on its local policy, may proceed to terminate the mobility session, because it then knows the anchor does not understand the option and may consider it a misconfiguration of the Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain.

On the anchor side, the conceptual Binding Cache entry must be extended with parameters for the Network-Identifier, the Geo-Location and the Operator-Identifier. On receiving a Proxy Binding Update with the option, the anchor must process it and update the corresponding fields in the Binding Cache entry; if the option is not understood, it will skip it. If the anchor understands the option and also supports the sub-options, it must echo the option back with the specific sub-options it accepted in the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement, and the sub-options defined in this specification must not be altered by the anchor. If the received Proxy Binding Update does not include the option, the mobility session must be updated to remove any access network information elements. The anchor may choose to use the sub-options for applying access-operator-specific handling or policing of the mobile node traffic, and the details of how are outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends have a switch for each piece of information, off by default. The gateway turns them on to include the information, the anchor turns them on to accept it, and the anchor sends back exactly what it accepted so the gateway knows the other side understood.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: Three IANA actions were completed. First, a new mobility header option, the Access Network Identifier, was defined, with the type value 52 assigned from the same numbering space as the other mobility options. Second, a new mobility sub-option format, the Access Network Information sub-option, was defined, with the type values managed by IANA under the registry for Access Network Information sub-option type values; the values 0 for reserved, 1 for the Network-Identifier sub-option, 2 for the Geo-Location sub-option and 3 for the Operator-Identifier sub-option are reserved by this specification, and approval of new values is through IANA Expert Review. Third, the Operator-Identifier sub-option introduces a new number space for the Op-ID Type field, managed under the Operator-Identifier Type Registry, with 0 reserved, 1 for an operator identifier as a variable-length Private Enterprise Number and 2 for the realm of the operator, again approved through IANA Expert Review.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps two short lists: the kinds of sub-option the option can hold, and the kinds of operator identifier. Both are worked out by expert review rather than by general agreement.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Access Network Information option is for use in Proxy Binding Update and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement messages, is carried like any other mobility header option, and does not require any special security considerations.

The Geo-Location sub-option exposes the geographic location of the network to which the mobile node is attached. This information is considered to be very sensitive, so care must be taken to secure the Proxy Mobile IPv6 signaling messages when carrying this sub-option. The base Proxy Mobile IPv6 specification specifies the use of IPsec for securing the signaling messages, and those mechanisms can be enabled to protect this information. Operators can potentially apply IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload with confidentiality and integrity protection for the location information.

Access-network-specific information elements that the mobile access gateway sends may have been dynamically learned over DHCP or using other protocols. If proper security mechanisms are not in place, the exchanged information may be compromised, with the mobile access gateway sending incorrect access network parameters to the local mobility anchor. That may result in incorrect service policy enforcement at the anchor and impact other services that depend on the access network information. The threat can be mitigated by ensuring the communication path between the mobile access gateway and the access points is properly secured by the use of IPsec, Transport Layer Security, or other security protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The option itself needs no special protection, but the location it can carry is private. Encrypt the signalling that carries it, and make sure the path the gateway learns the access network details over cannot be tampered with.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Must be 52, identifying the Access Network Identifier option.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the option, excluding the Type and Length fields. The sub-options follow.

items.label: Network-Identifier sub-option
items.desc: The name of the access network and the access point.

items.label: Geo-Location sub-option
items.desc: The latitude and longitude of the network.

items.label: Operator-Identifier sub-option
items.desc: The identity of the operator running the network.

fields.name: ANI Type
fields.desc: Must be 2, indicating the Geo-Location sub-option.

fields.name: Latitude Degrees
fields.desc: Two's complement fixed point with 9 whole bits, from -90 to +90 degrees.

fields.name: Longitude Degrees
fields.desc: Two's complement fixed point with 9 whole bits, from -180 to +180 degrees.

items.label: Private Enterprise Number
items.desc: A variable-length PEN in network byte order. The largest value is 2^((ANI_length-1)*8)-1, so an ANI Length of 4 allows 0 to 16777215.

items.label: Realm of the operator
items.desc: A DNS realm name, encoded as US-ASCII.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH END DOES WITH THE OPTION

cells: Extends the Binding Update List entry with the Network-Identifier, Operator-Identifier and Geo-Location
Extends the Binding Cache entry with the Network-Identifier, Geo-Location and Operator-Identifier
Should include the option in Proxy Binding Update messages when configured to
Must echo back the sub-options it accepted, unaltered
Should log the event and may terminate the session
Must remove any access network information from the session

items.title: The location is sensitive
items.text: The Geo-Location sub-option reveals where the network is, so the signalling carrying it should be protected with IPsec.

items.title: The information may be wrong
items.text: If the path the gateway learns the access details over is not secured, a bad value can lead to the wrong policy being applied.

items.title: The option itself needs nothing special
items.text: It is carried like any other mobility header option, so no additional security rules apply to it.
